source.citation: C. Seymour, "Erythromelalgia," Medical Record 37 (1890): 656. First name and place to confirm from the page image.

reported.label: Miss A. B.
reported.familyHistory: Mother a nervous invalid; otherwise good.

complaints: sudden burning pain in the ball of the left foot when walking, spreading to the top of the foot and the leg
cannot stand or let the foot hang down; at ease only with the foot raised
the foot swells and turns a mottled red when the pain comes
presentation.course: Seven years ago gave up teaching for two years with neurasthenia from overwork. Used chloral for insomnia then, and has slept with chloral or sulfonal for five years since, even after returning to work. The foot pain began eighteen months ago on a walk.
presentation.priorTreatment: Self-continued chloral and sulfonal for sleep.

findings: well developed and well nourished; fair, florid complexion
no hysterical constitution, in the author's view
during pain the foot is swollen and mottled red, with little tenderness to pressure
periodDiagnosis: erythromelalgia (Weir Mitchell's vasomotor neurosis), in a former neurasthenic with a chloral habit
quotes: her health became im- paired from excessive mental application, and she had to relinquish work for two years, wrestling with neurasthenia
For five years she has slept either with chloral or its recent congener, sulfonal.

modernReading.text: Erythromelalgia, a real disorder of small vessels and nerves, sometimes linked to blood disorders or small-fibre neuropathy. The long hypnotic use is a separate dependence problem a doctor should notice.

fixed: burning, red, swollen foot brought on by standing or warmth and eased by raising it
years of nightly chloral or sulfonal begun during a breakdown

constrained.rule: brain-work with a past breakdown from overwork: teacher, governess, clerk, writer
comfortable or affluent; can buy hypnotics regularly
the patient does not volunteer the hypnotic habit; she presents only the foot

notes: Two problems in one patient: the complaint she brings and the habit she does not mention. Treatment and outcome are later in the article and not yet read.
